title: Man saw doctor before rampage: Stittsville father killed by police battled depression and brain tumour
article: The Stittsville father who was shot dead by police after he stabbed his wife and two neighbours visited the emergency room of the Royal Ottawa Hospital in the week before his death and was given a new prescription by a family doctor the day before he snapped.
Frank Hutterer, 35, had been battling depression for several years before police killed him in front of his Cordukes Street bungalow Wednesday morning.
He had gone to the emergency room at the Royal Ottawa Hospital last week.
As is standard procedure at the hospital, he was assessed by a physician. The doctor recommended Mr. Hutterer admit himself to stay at the hospital.
Mr. Hutterer instead went home. He told his wife, 34-year-old Sally McIntyre, that speaking with the doctor had lifted his sagging spirits.
On Tuesday, Mr. Hutterer visited another doctor and was prescribed a new medication.
The next morning, he lost his mind.
As his wife prepared their son, eight-year-old Benjamin, for school, Mr. Hutterer confronted her in a violent rage she had never seen before.

A heated argument ensued and Ms. McIntyre urged Benjamin to leave and walk to school by himself. Moments after Benjamin began walking to school for the first time alone, without his father at his side, Mr. Hutterer grabbed two butcher knives and attacked his wife.
She broke free and scrambled across the road to the home of their elderly neighbours, Mitch Smith, 71, and his wife, Margaret, 69.
Mr. Hutterer followed with a knife in each hand, chanting in a high pitch, "You are dead! You are dead!"
He cornered his wife at the door in the Smiths' car port and stabbed her repeatedly, his chilling death chant never ceasing. Mr. and Mrs. Smith intervened, and Mr. Hutterer stabbed them as well.
When Ottawa-Carleton police arrived, Mr. Hutterer lunged at a female officer with his blades. She shot him once, but it had little effect.
When he continued toward her, she shot him three more times in rapid succession, and he dropped dead at the foot of the Smiths' driveway.
All those who knew and loved him said Mr. Hutterer's sudden murderous rage was completely out of line with the gentle, calm demeanour he had always possessed.
"Sally said he hadn't been feeling well in the last two weeks," brother Brian Hutterer said.
"He ended up going to the hospital and he told Sally he was feeling better, but he just kept going in and out of these stages.
"We're not sure what pills he was taking, whether they were to treat his depression or something else. But he did seek help. We've all been too shocked to look for any answers at this point."

Mr. Hutterer's parents, John and Pat, received news of their son's death while on vacation in Austria. They arrived in Ottawa yesterday to visit their son's widow at the Ottawa Hospital's Civic site, where she remained in fair condition.

"I'm just numb," Mrs. Hutterer said. "That wasn't our Frankie. It was a great marriage. He never laid a hand on her the whole 11 years of their married life. I've never seen him speak an angry word to her. He was a wonderful boy, and he loved her."

Mr. Hutterer battled depression off and on as a young adult and in his final years. About four years ago, doctors discovered a tumour on the optical nerve in his brain. Once surgeons began the operation, they determined it was too risky to try to remove it.

The rare condition caused Mr. Hutterer to lose most of his sight in one eye, and surgeons feared a biopsy would have caused permanent blindness in both eyes. He underwent MRIs every six months to monitor the tumour.
An autopsy has been completed, but Mrs. Hutterer said it will be several weeks before doctors are able to determine what may have happened.
Dr. Marv Lange, director of clinical services at the ROH, said patients who check themselves into emergency can't be forced to stay.

"When people come to the emergency room, they are given an assessment by a physician, who generally offers a range of treatments," Dr. Lange said. "One of those would be admission to the hospital. But that, in most cases, would require the patient's agreement. At the other end of the scale, it may involve giving some advice to a family physician. The advice to the family physician may include giving the patient a prescription."

The hospital's emergency room, which closed permanently Wednesday, admitted an average of 1,200 mentally ill patients each year. Future emergency patients will now be re-routed to the Ottawa Hospital's Civic and General sites.
Mr. Hutterer's family is planning a private funeral service in Alliston, Ont., for Wednesday.
